Introduction

[
1
]

The plaintiff, aptly known as “O.W.L.”, is a
charitable society whose purpose is to rescue and care for injured raptors,
such as owls and eagles, and promote their recovery and return to the wild. The
defendant, Beverly Day, was O.W.L.’s founder. Her longstanding employment as
O.W.L.’s executive director was terminated by the Board of Directors on October
23, 2014, without notice and allegedly for cause.

[
2
]

O.W.L. advanced three grounds for the termination
of Ms. Day’s employment at the time of her dismissal. The first, which is
at the heart of this action, is O.W.L.’s assertion that Ms. Day misappropriated
its funds to pay for the cost of her housing. The other two grounds concerned
her dealings with two of O.W.L.’s full-time employees - her dismissal of Rob
Hope and remarks she is alleged to have made to Martina Versteed.

[
3
]

O.W.L. commenced this lawsuit on January 13,
2015. It sued Ms. Day for breach of contract, asserting that she failed in
her contractual duty to ensure that O.W.L.’s bookkeeper deduct her rent from
her paycheques and failed to reimburse O.W.L. for those payments. Throughout this
action, up until the start of closing argument, O.W.L. characterized Ms. Day’s
conduct as misappropriation. O.W.L. also advanced an alternative claim for
unjust enrichment.

[
4
]

Ms. Day denied the claim and filed a
counterclaim seeking damages for wrongful dismissal. After Ms. Day’s counterclaim
was filed on February 16, 2015, O.W.L. responded with additional grounds for
termination in its response pleading, alleging in part, additional
misappropriation or unjust enrichment (in paying herself unauthorized salary
and vacation pay) and insubordination.

[
5
]

The trial of the parties’ dispute was adjourned
twice due to the unavailability of a trial judge. When the case did proceed to
trial in April 2018, O.W.L. continued to advance its misappropriation claim until
the start of closing argument on May 12, 2018. At that point, O.W.L. advised
that it was abandoning that claim (and corresponding defence to the
counterclaim). O.W.L. now relies solely on its alternative claim against Ms. Day
for unjust enrichment. O.W.L. nonetheless continues to allege financial
mismanagement on Ms. Day’s part in its defence to her claim for wrongful
dismissal, alleging that she “closed her eyes” to what it alleges was
unauthorized payments of her rent “and did so purposely”.

[
6
]

This was not the only change in position taken
by O.W.L. in the case. In its notice of civil claim, O.W.L. alleged that Ms. Day
was always obliged to pay for her own rent and that she had failed to ensure
that her rent was paid and as a result, received unauthorized rent payments “since
at least 2006”. It later amended its pleading to allege that she failed to
ensure her rent was deducted from her paycheques since January 1, 2007. At one
point in the case, O.W.L. sought recovery for unauthorized payments valued at $174,390.50,
based in part upon a report prepared for O.W.L. by a chartered accountant. When
the trial began, O.W.L. advised that it was not tendering the report and that
the claim was reduced to just over $64,000.

[
7
]

O.W.L.’s own documents and the evidence of its
former bookkeepers clearly demonstrate that there never was any basis for O.W.L.’s
claims that Ms. Day received unauthorized payments. Ms. Day’s
employment was wrongly terminated, without cause, because O.W.L’s Board of Directors
(“Board”) rushed to judgment and assumed the worst possible construction of
alleged events involving Ms. Day, having carried out only a partial and
scant investigation. The reasons put forward by the Board at the time of Ms. Day’s
termination were factually inaccurate and did not justify her dismissal.

[
8
]

My findings of fact are set out throughout these
reasons for judgment. For that reason, I will not repeat that they are my
findings.

Background Facts

[
9
]

Ms. Day is 68 years old. She became
involved in bird recovery and rehabilitation prior to her incorporation of
O.W.L. as a charitable society in 1985. Prior to O.W.L.’s incorporation, Ms. Day
operated a bird recovery program out of her small home. She used her own money
to care for birds. Through self-study, and with the support of her second husband,
Jim Day, (deceased) and help from local veterinarians who volunteered their
time, she learned about bird care for raptors over time. Her reputation and
work spread throughout the province and, ultimately, beyond provincial and
federal boundaries. People brought their injured birds to her to be cared for.
Police officers and firefighters regularly brought injured raptors they found
to her for care. Through her dedication and hard work over a 40-year period, Ms. Day
has built her bird care program and O.W.L. into an internationally renowned raptor
rehabilitation and education facility, currently occupying several buildings
(including converted barns) on approximately five acres of land in Delta, B.C.
O.W.L. is assisted by full-time and part-time employees and many volunteers.

[
10
]

Bird care and O.W.L. have therefore been Ms. Day’s
key focus for most of her adult life. It is an understatement to say that Ms. Day
is passionate about the care and well-being of raptors and the reputation and
success of O.W.L. Her home life when growing up was fractured and at times
abusive. She lived in foster care for a time and left school early when she
decided to support herself at different jobs, including housecleaning and working
for a large family with 10 children and later, serving in a bar and a
restaurant, and then, in her 20s, as a traffic flagger. Ms. Day began
looking after birds while working as a flagger. She did not complete high
school. She had a daughter when she was just under 18 years old.

[
11
]

Prior to becoming involved with bird care, Ms. Day
had no training or experience operating a business. She has no training as an
accountant or bookkeeper. Her experience with and knowledge of bookkeeping is
rudimentary at best.

[
12
]

Ms. Day quickly found herself working full-time
caring for birds, which she and her husband did out of their home. She was also
on call throughout the night as she received telephone calls from the police,
firefighters, and others informing her of injured raptors (often found
roadside) to be picked up for care. She tried to limit the number of days she
worked as a flagger in order to focus on bird care, by working evenings, which
credited her with additional hours and just enough income to meet expenses. The
small house she lived in with Jim Day was consumed with bird care and related
activities. When Mr. and Ms. Day later found themselves without work,
they could no longer afford to pay the expenses for bird care. They decided to
incorporate as a charitable society in order to raise money through donations
to fund the operation. Pending donations sufficient to fund the expenses, Ms. and
Mr. Day sold a camper and a truck, made and sold crafts and window boxes
at local markets, and raised money by selling donated items at garage sales.
Their landlord was also kind enough to let them fall behind in their rent for a
few months.

[
13
]

Over time, assisted by news and television
publicity, Ms. Day secured food and equipment donations to care for the
birds. O.W.L.’s revenue is derived from donations. O.W.L. grew to the point
where she need more space for the birds, cages, and other equipment and
supplies. O.W.L. eventually moved to its present (leased) premises at a larger
location in Delta with a number of empty buildings in need of repair. With the
help of volunteers, Ms. Day fixed up the buildings over time, setting up
separate facilities for emergency bird care, a treatment centre, housing for
birds in recovery, and an office. Ms. Day also set up an educational
program which she ran on site (in her home until she obtained a grant to
convert a portable structure into an on-site education centre). Ms. Day
also conducted off-site educational programs throughout her tenure at O.W.L. Its
education programs were provided for students of all ages. Ms. Day also established
a formal volunteer program. As O.W.L.’s operations grew, it hired staff who
worked in bird care and the office. Ms. Day’s responsibilities grew as
O.W.L. did. She oversaw its increasing operations, continued in her prodigious
and ongoing fund raising efforts, and continued to speak at public events and
to the media in order to raise O.W.L.’s profile. She worked with staff in a
separate office building when she was not in the field or working off site.

[
14
]

Ms. Day was a forceful personality at
O.W.L. She was well known at O.W.L. and to its Board for her strong opinions,
straightforward style of communication, and personal interest in the well-being
of its staff and volunteers. She was admired as the driving force and moral
spirit of O.W.L. Public relations came naturally to Ms. Day. She was well
liked by the public she dealt with and excelled in fundraising.

[
15
]

Throughout Ms. Day’s tenure, O.W.L.’s lease with
its landlord (which ultimately became known as the Delta Community Living
Society) required someone to remain on site at all times. The Board wanted Ms. Day
to live on site as O.W.L.’s caretaker. Ms. Day lived in a separate residence
on site. In May 2002, she moved to a smaller house on the property (a pre-fabricated
mobile building affixed to the land) when the landlord required her existing
residence for its own purposes. Both of her residences were used for O.W.L.’s
business up until the point when Ms. Day’s employment was terminated, including
after hours care for rescued birds. Both before and after O.W.L.’s
incorporation, and even after O.W.L.’s physical operations grew in size, Ms. Day’s
home was used for bird care (such as emergency medical treatment for birds and
housing rescued birds in different sized cages) and related activities. Board
meetings were also held in her home before O.W.L. established an office in a
separate building. Except for the few instances where Ms. Day was
physically out of the Lower Mainland and unable to respond to emergencies, she
was on call 24 hours a day, seven days a week, even on her scheduled days off. Since
O.W.L. dealt mainly with raptors, which are nocturnal animals, most of the
emergency calls came in at night. When Ms. Day was away from O.W.L.’s
premises overnight, another person would be paid to live in her residence and
be on call.

Ms. Day’s Employment with
O.W.L.

[
16
]

When O.W.L. incorporated, Ms. Day became a
member of the Board and continued to run its operations. She was paid a stipend.
The rest of the Board was comprised of volunteers who donated their time. Ms. Day
recruited board members with different areas of expertise such as accounting, business
management and operations, and government (e.g., a member of the legislative
assembly who was also a provincial minister of agriculture).

[
17
]

Later, when O.W.L. learned that a member of the
Board could not be paid as an employee, the Board and Ms. Day agreed to
change her status to executive director and chief operations officer with a paid
salary. She was no longer a member of the Board. She was, however, required to
attend Board meetings and provide reports on O.W.L.’s operations. She was not
permitted to vote. Her responsibilities did not change. She worked at least
five days per week and as mentioned above, was on call 24 hours per day and on her
days off work. In addition to running O.W.L.’s operations overall, Ms. Day
regularly worked at the education centre, led tours, submitted applications for
government grants, lectured to groups and organizations off site, and organized
and led fund-raising activities. She related well to people, including O.W.L.’s
staff and volunteers, and also to members, donors, and potential donors. She
was closely involved in all aspects of O.W.L.’s operations and business
affairs.

[
18
]

Ms. Day testified that she entered into a
written employment agreement with O.W.L. but is unable to find it. From her
recollection, she said that one of the terms required the Board to take any
issues or concerns about her employment to a panel of her peers for
adjudication and from there, to a vote at an O.W.L. annual general meeting
(“AGM”). According to Ms. Day, one of O.W.L.’s directors suggested this
clause be included in her employment contract for her benefit. The existence of
this term in Ms. Day’s contract was alluded to by a former president and prior
longstanding director of O.W.L., Ms. Lynn Short, in a letter she wrote to
the Board dated November 1, 2014. In the absence of reviewing the written
contract and any corroborating Board minutes, I am not able to make any finding
that this term was part of Ms. Day’s employment contract given the
tentative nature of the
viva voce
evidence on the point. However, support
for Ms. Day’s evidence that she had a written contract with O.W.L. is
found in Board minutes from January 16, 1995 where the need to “write up”
contracts for all paid employees is noted.

[
19
]

Despite the absence of the written agreement, I
was able to determine its core terms from various sources, such as Board
meeting minutes, Ms. Day’s evidence (which I found candid, reliable, and
credible), past and present Board members, and one of O.W.L.’s former bookkeepers,
Ms. Irene Hill.

[
20
]

In addition to overseeing the operations of O.W.L.
and reporting to the Board as I have described thus far, and apart from Ms. Day’s
remuneration which I will discuss in the next section, the material terms of Ms. Day’s
employment contract are as follows:

(a)

Her working hours were full-time, five days per
week, plus on call after hours throughout evenings and nights. Her scheduled
days off varied from time to time.

(b)

It was expected that if Ms. Day was on site
on her scheduled days off of work, she would be available on call to handle
emergencies, including those involving injured birds.

(c)

Ms. Day had the unfettered authority to
hire, supervise, discipline, and fire employees.

(d)

She was responsible for fund raising and public
relations.

(e)

Ms. Day would reside in separate
accommodation located on site.

(f)

She liaised with O.W.L.’s staff, notably its
supervisors.

(g)

She reported to the Board at regularly scheduled
Board meetings and as required in the interim.

[
21
]

Some of Ms. Day’s job duties are also
described in Board minutes dated June 26, 2004:

BEV’S  JOB DESCRIPTION:

-

Fund raising

-

Public relations

-

Liaise with supervisors and office personnel

-

On-call after hours

-

Report to board on general and extraordinary
events

-

Complaint department (should Bev in fact be
doing this?)

-

Medical training of staff

-

Has ultimate decision re bird care

[
22
]

Ms. Day was not responsible for O.W.L.’s
finances or its bookkeeping. In her testimony, Ms. Wheatley, who is
O.W.L.’s current president and self-admitted driving force in O.W.L.’s
litigation against Ms. Day, attempted in her evidence to add accounting to
Ms. Day’s job duties because she saw Ms. Day sitting with one of O.W.L.’s
bookkeepers, Irene Hill, going over staff payroll. As I point out in these
reasons, I found this to be part of her
ad hoc
and oftentimes disingenuous
attempts to reconstruct events to O.W.L.’s advantage when it was clearly
inconsistent with other credible and reliable evidence and not supported by
documents, including minutes of Board meetings.

[
23
]

O.W.L. relied on volunteer bookkeepers to maintain
its books and records, track expenditures in relation to O.W.L.’s budget, issue
cheques including paycheques, prepare and submit applications for government
grants for summer students, and prepare financial statements for review by the
Board, including the Board’s treasurer. Its bookkeepers worked for accounting
firms and routinely took their year-end financial statements to senior
accountants at their firms for review. Ms. Day would, from time to time,
take deposits to the bank but she was not responsible for, participate in, nor
have the acumen to maintain O.W.L.’s financial records, including payroll. She
did not sign her own cheques. Her paycheques were prepared by O.W.L.’s bookkeepers
and signed by other authorized signatories approved by the Board.

[
24
]

One of O.W.L.’s past presidents, Ms. Lynn Short,
whose evidence I accept, testified that directions to O.W.L.’s bookkeepers concerning
salary and benefits came from the Board.

[
25
]

According to O.W.L.’s constitution, overall
responsibility for O.W.L.’s finances rested with the Board, and in particular,
its treasurer. Its constitution, established under the
Society Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 433 [
Society Act
] provides, in Part 7, concerning
the duties of officers:

42.       The treasurer shall

(a)        keep
such financial records, including books of account, as are necessary to comply
with the
Society Act
, and

(b)        render
financial statements to the Directors, members and others when required.

…

51.       The Directors, on behalf of the
Society, shall keep proper accounting records in respect of all financial or
other transactions and, without limiting the foregoing, shall keep records of:

(a)        all
money received and disbursed by the Society and the matter in respect of which
the receipt and disbursement took place;

(b)        every
asset and liability of the Society;

(c)        every other
transaction affecting the financial position of the Society.

[
26
]

Insofar as its lease was concerned, O.W.L. also relied
on the advice of a lawyer who volunteered her time to review the terms of the
lease provided by the landlord. Board members were involved in lease
negotiations and Ms. Day did not conduct them on her own. There is no
merit to the suggestion raised during trial that Ms. Day engaged in lease
negotiations with the landlord to the exclusion of the Board that permitted her
to shield from the Board’s view the amount allocated for the rent of her
premises or the manner in which it was being paid.

O.W.L.’s Claim for Unauthorized
Payments

[
27
]

O.W.L.’s claim against Ms. Day concerns unauthorized
payments it alleges she received for the rent allocated to her on-site housing,
salary, and vacation pay. O.W.L. also relied on its claim as a defence to Ms. Day’s
counterclaim. The claim and the defence, as pleaded and as O.W.L. attempted to
modify it during the trial, are without merit.

Ms. Day’s Remuneration

Introductory Remarks

[
28
]

I will begin with my findings concerning Ms. Day’s
global remuneration from O.W.L., including my finding that O.W.L. was obliged
throughout to pay the rent attributed to Ms. Day’s on-site housing as part
of it.

[
29
]

Ms. Day was not permitted any decision-making
authority in respect to any aspect of her remuneration. She was not allowed to
attend Board meetings when her remuneration was discussed, nor was her current
husband, Ralph Smith, who was also a Board member, when the key events that led
up to Ms. Day’s dismissal occurred. All aspects of Ms. Day’s remuneration,
including salary, vacation pay, and housing, were made by the Board.
Responsibility rested with the Board for those decisions, which were then
carried out by O.W.L.’s bookkeepers in accordance with what they understood to
be the Board’s instructions, generally accepted accounting practices, and the
law.

[
30
]

The rent issue, originally grounded in
misappropriation, was one of three specific grounds conveyed to Ms. Day for
her dismissal. O.W.L.’s notice of civil claim, both as initially filed and as
amended, alleges that it was always Ms. Day’s obligation to pay for that
portion of O.W.L.’s lease allocated to Ms. Day’s on-site accommodation. In
its amended notice of civil claim filed on May 26, 2016, over a year after it
commenced this lawsuit, O.W.L. alleged, in part:

18.       The Defendant in her role as
executive director was responsible for negotiating the terms of the lease of
the Plaintiff’s business premises. The Defendant resided in a home on the
premises of the Plaintiff’s business. The agreement
at all times
between
the Plaintiff and the Defendant was that the Defendant would be personally
responsible for the rent attributable to her personal residence. When the
Defendant negotiated the terms of the lease with the landlord, specific
allocation of the amount attributable to her personal residence was made. …

[Emphasis added].

[
31
]

O.W.L.’s case is also pleaded on the basis that Ms. Day
instructed O.W.L.’s bookkeepers to deduct the rent from all of Ms. Day’s
paycheques but failed to do so:

20.       The Defendant provided
instructions to a book keeper who prepared the checks for pay roll, including
the Defendant’s checks. Those instructions included the deductions which were
to be made
from all pay checks
. The Defendant failed to instruct the
book keeper to deduct the $650 from her pay check attributable to the rent of
her personal residence. The Defendant did not in any other manner reimburse the
Plaintiff for the $650 per month attributable to her rent.
This was
purposeful action on the part of the Defendant to wrongfully cause the
Plaintiff to pay on her behalf the rent of her personal residence.

[Emphasis added.]

[
32
]

In closing argument, O.W.L. changed its
position, alleging that its agreement with Ms. Day originally called for
it to pay for her rent, but that the agreement later changed. It pointed to another
paragraph - 22 - in its amended pleading as supporting its position that Ms. Day
was obliged to pay for rent starting in January 2007. However, that pleading
refers only to a date which O.W.L. alleges Ms. Day failed to ensure that
her rent was deducted from her paycheques. It does not refer to any alteration
of Ms. Day’s employment agreement.

[
33
]

One of the submissions made on behalf of Ms. Day
in closing argument is that O.W.L.’s claim should be dismissed outright because
it failed to adduce any evidence in support of the claim as pleaded. Counsel
for Ms. Day went further and submitted that in its case, O.W.L. adduced
contradictory and inconsistent evidence concerning the allegation.

[
34
]

I agree that O.W.L. led evidence contradicting
its pleaded allegation that the obligation to pay her rent always fell on Ms. Day,
and in that respect, it also adduced inconsistent evidence from two Board
members, Ms. Lita Wells and Ms. Karen Wheatley.

[
35
]

Ms. Lita Wells was a Board member at different
times. She joined the Board when O.W.L. was incorporated as a society. She was
also a Board member when the key events immediately surrounding Ms. Day’s
dismissal occurred. Contrary to O.W.L.’s pleading, Ms. Wells testified that the
agreement with Ms. Day concerning her rent changed in 2002. At that time, she
said, O.W.L. was no longer responsible to pay for Ms. Day’s rent.

[
36
]

Ms. Wells presented as a stiff, scripted, and
inappropriately stubborn, argumentative, and unyielding witness who would not
admit to her mistakes in recollection of key matters when confronted with
O.W.L.’s own documents. At times, she resorted to a tone inflected with sarcasm
when confronted with documents such as Board minutes contradicting her evidence-in-chief.

[
37
]

Ms. Wells was also confused about certain
key events and dates, including the dates of her tenure as a Board member and
the timing of Board meetings to decide on the termination of Ms. Day’s
employment with O.W.L.

[
38
]

Ms. Wells’ evidence concerning Ms. Day’s
remuneration was not only inconsistent with O.W.L.’s pleading concerning the
misappropriation of rent claim, I found it to be incorrect with Board minutes
and unreliable. For example, she said she did not know what Ms. Day was
being paid, adding that the Board was very rarely provided with that
information (although she said at one point in her evidence-in-chief that she “believed”
she approved an increase in Ms. Day’s salary “once or twice”). The Board
minutes (which I review in a later section) shows that Ms. Wells’ evidence
is incorrect in these respects. The Board was informed of Ms. Day’s salary on a
regular basis. When some of the minutes showing Board approved increases to Ms.
Day’s salary were put to her in cross-examination, Ms. Wells conceded that
there may have been additional increases, yet in spite of the minutes,
maintained that she could not be certain. In terms of the rent claim, Ms. Wells
could not say whether O.W.L. was paying for Ms. Day’s rent at its prior
premises yet she was adamant that the arrangement with Ms. Day changed in
May 2002 (not 2007) when the Board required her to pay her rent. Not only is
this inconsistent with O.W.L.’s pleading as well as its revised position
advanced during closing argument, it is inconsistent with Board minutes and the
evidence of other former O.W.L. directors who gave clear and reliable accounts
of key past events. After hearing all of Ms. Wells’ evidence, I concluded
that she had no actual recollection of the facts concerning Ms. Day’s
remuneration and has endeavoured to rely upon information provided to her about
the rent issue and other alleged unauthorized payments.

[
39
]

Ms. Wheatley’s role on the Board is more
recent. She joined the Board in April 2011. She has no direct personal involvement
or knowledge of the Board’s prior decisions regarding Ms. Day’s
remuneration. Board minutes reflect her first attendance at a Board meeting to
be July 10, 2011. However, that did not prevent Ms. Wheatley from engaging
in argument while giving evidence, as she sought to construe Board minutes from
July 2007 (she was not on the Board at that time) to support her view of
matters and to provide evidence that she thought would buttress O.W.L.’s case
and defence to the counterclaim. Ms. Wheatley contradicted Ms. Wells

Evidence of Past Board Members and

[
53
]

Four previous Board members - Anita Phillips,

Anita Phillips

[

[

]

but no formal education as a bookkeeper. She learned on the job from past

]

[
92
]

At the time she was dismissed, Ms. Day was
paid $41,424.00 (gross), plus five weeks’ vacation.

93
]

94
]

evidence in cross-examination when she was forced to agree that her evidence concerning

after

2002, O.W.L. treated part of the rent as a taxable benefit. Ms. Wheatley’s

I thought, okay,
well, we’re giving, you know, our landlord just one cheque, so you know, it

[

Determination of Unauthorized Rent
Claim

[
101
]

Ms. Day’s rent was paid for by O.W.L. as part of her employment
contract. O.W.L. agreed to pay it throughout the whole of Ms. Day’s
employment. There was no credible or reliable evidence to contradict the Board
minutes and the evidence of former Board members and O.W.L.’s bookkeepers. There
was no alteration to O.W.L.’s obligation to pay Ms. Day’s rent. Ms. Day is
not obliged to reimburse O.W.L. for the cost of the rent allocated to her
on-site premises. O.W.L.’s claim for unjust enrichment is dismissed.

[
102
]

I will conclude this section with four observations.

[
103
]

The first is that O.W.L. had access to its Board minutes and its former
bookkeepers prior to trial. Its bookkeepers testified that they were contacted
on behalf of O.W.L. prior to trial. Even if O.W.L. was not able to obtain their
evidence prior to trial, O.W.L. was fully aware of it as well as Board minutes
and the evidence of past Board members during the trial and nonetheless chose

[
104
]

The second is that O.W.L. persisted in maintaining allegations of
financial mismanagement against Ms. Day through to the conclusion of the

[
105
]

The third concerns a with prejudice offer contained in O.W.L.’s

took what they characterized as Ms. Day’s intentional misconduct in
misappropriating funds that had been donated to O.W.L. from individual and
corporate donors and government grants.

[
106
]

The fourth is that in assessing the evidence adduced by the parties
in respect of O.W.L.’s claim, as well as the counterclaim, and in evaluating

Faryna
v. Chorny
,
1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA)
, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 (B.C.C.A.). I also find the comments made by
Mr. Justice Davies in
Chudy v. Merchant Law Group
,
2007 BCSC 279
at
para.
57
, that documents created at the time events occurred offer far more
reliable evidence of what occurred as opposed to attempts at present

of the

Case Law

[
141
]

An employer is entitled to dismiss an employee for just cause when
the latter’s conduct is incompatible with those duties that go to the root of
the employment contract, and results in a fracturing of the employment
relationship to such an extent that the employer cannot be expected to provide
the employee with a second chance. The employee’s behaviour must be seriously
incompatible with his or her duties:
Leung v. Doppler Industries, Inc.
(1995),

1995 CanLII 2530 (BC SC)
, 10 C.C.E.L. (2d) 147 at paras.
26-27
(B.C.S.C.);
Panton v. Everywoman’s Health
Centre Society
(1988)
,
2000 BCCA 621
at para.
28
;
Steel v. Coast
Capital Savings Credit Union
,
2015 BCCA 127
;
Kerr v. Arpac Storage
Systems Corp.
,
2018 BCSC 704
at para.
53
.

[
142
]

In determining whether just cause has been established, the court
must examine the circumstances surrounding the alleged misconduct and its
degree. Context is important, and includes the nature of the employment
contract in issue and the status of the employee:
McKinley v. BC Tel
,

2001 SCC 38
at paras.
33-34
, 51;
Kerr
at para.
54
.

[
143
]

The onus rests on the employer to establish it had just cause to
dismiss the employee:
Staley v. Squirrel Systems of Canada
,
Ltd.
,

2013 BCCA 201
at para.19, citing
Leung
at para.
26
;
Kerr

at para.
52
;

Horvath v. SAAN Stores Ltd.
,
2003 BCSC 1845
at para.
2
. In
Staley
,
the Court of Appeal described the onus as a “heavy one”: para. 19.

[
144
]

The suitability of alternative disciplinary measures to address the
impugned conduct must be considered by the employer before taking the most
severe form of reprimand step possible, which is to fire the employee and deny
him or her with a means of financial support. An effective balance must be
sought by the employer between the severity of the alleged misconduct and the
sanction imposed:
McKinley
at para.
53
;
Kerr

at para.
56
.
Progressive discipline, usually starting with clear and unequivocal warnings, followed
by suspensions prior to dismissal is the usual course:
Bomford v. Wayden
Transportation Systems Inc.
,
2010 BCSC 1506
at paras.
6-9
;
Hennessy
v. Excell Railing Systems Ltd.
,
2005 BCSC 734
at paras.
12-14
;
Laszczewski
v. Aluminart Products Limited
(2007),
2007 CanLII 56493 (ON SC)
, 62 C.C.E.L. (3d) 305 (Ont. S.C.J.).

[
145
]

There were no prior incidents of concern about Ms. Day’s
performance of her job duties identified in O.W.L.’s case, and she had not
received any warnings or hints of warnings of issues concerning her employment,
let alone that it might be terminated.

[
146
]

In
McKinley
, the Supreme Court of Canada
remarked on the importance of proportionality:

[53]      Underlying the approach I propose
is the principle of proportionality. An effective balance must be struck
between the severity of an employee’s misconduct and the sanction imposed. The
importance of this balance is better understood by considering the sense of
identity and self-worth individuals frequently derive from their employment, a
concept that was explored in
Reference Re Public Service Employee Relations
Act (Alta.)
,
1987 CanLII 88 (SCC)
, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 313, where Dickson C.J. (writing in dissent)
stated at p. 368:

Work is one of the most fundamental aspects

identity and sense of self-worth is intimately tied with her longstanding

proportionality in any sense before it dismissed Ms. Day. It failed to

investigation, the Board assumed the worst of Ms. Day’s conduct when it

at para.

[14]      In my
view, the requirement of a contextual approach and an analysis of the nature
and circumstances of the misconduct established by McKinley places an onus on a
defendant asserting just cause to take a similar contextual approach in its
investigation of misconduct and in its determination of the appropriate
sanction. Where the investigation conducted in the first instance by a
defendant asserting just cause is insufficiently broad to establish the full
nature and circumstances of the misconduct and thereby the ability of the court
to conduct the sort of analysis envisaged in McKinley is impaired, it follows
that the defendant will similarly be impaired in discharging its onus of proof
in connection with its claim of just cause.

]

The Board Sticks to its
Determination to Pay Severance

[
205
]

Faced with Ms. Day’s jurisdictional objection to its earlier
vote, the Board held a directors’ only meeting on September 7, 2014, to vote on

to the meeting. It is not clear whether Mr. Smith was invited or intentionally

[
206
]

After the meeting, Lita Wells then sent copies of documents she had
from her own files, including warning documents handed to Mr. Hope and the

although in reading the written opinion from O.W.L.’s lawyer, which is in
evidence, it appears that she was not provided with all of the relevant
background facts.

[
207
]

Instead of wanting to ensure that relevant facts be obtained and
provided to O.W.L.’s lawyer, Ms. Wheatley testified that she was most
unhappy that Ms. Wells provided this information to O.W.L.’s lawyer since Ms. Wheatley
(erroneously) believed that the documents were given to Ms. Wells by Ms. Day
in order to buttress her view of Mr. Hope’s case and interfere with the
Board’s dealings with its lawyer (as mentioned, those documents came from Ms. Wells’
file).

[
208
]

The Board met again on September 21, 2014. Ms. Day was invited
to attend this meeting. The legal opinion of counsel recommending that
severance be paid was circulated by Ms. Wheatley. Ms. Day continued
to object.

[
209
]

There is a conflict in the evidence adduced in O.W.L.’s case as to
whether Ms. Day was instructed to open a filing cabinet located in
O.W.L.’s office and produce O.W.L.’s chequebook for the Board to sign a
severance cheque payable to Mr. Hope or whether Ms. Day was told to
sign the cheque itself. There is also a conflict in the evidence as to when the
incident involving the filing cabinet and chequebook occurred, with Mr. Hutchison
wavering as to the number of times the Board made the request of Ms. Day
and when. As mentioned, I do not accept Mr. Hutchison’s evidence because
it was given as the result of prompting that moved at times to leading as he
tried to suggest that she refused to open the cabinet on more than one
occasion.

Refusing to Open the Cabinet

[
210
]

My findings in respect of the filing cabinet and chequebook incident
are as follows.

[
211
]

The incident occurred on Sunday, September 21, 2014 during a Board
meeting. Ms. Day was asked to open the filing cabinet where the chequebook
was kept so that a cheque could be written to Mr. Hope to pay him
severance. Two signatures are required on all of O.W.L.’s cheques. O.W.L.’s
bookkeeper as well as Ms. Day and certain Board members (including Ms. Wheatley)
are authorized signatories. Many of O.W.L.’s cheques were pre-signed with one
signature from an authorized person. Ms. Day protested, asserting that she
acted appropriately and that Mr. Hope did not deserve to be compensated.
The Board demanded that she immediately open the cabinet in order for the Board
to obtain the chequebook. She refused, believing in good conscience that no
severance should be paid. She told the Board that it “wasn’t right” and asked
that the Board wait for two days, until Tuesday. She was particularly concerned
that funds from donors sitting in bank accounts allocated would be improperly
accessed to pay for the severance. Ms. Day believed that if Mr. Hope took
the matter to “labour relations” and advised them of the facts, including his
prior warnings, his claim for severance would be denied. The Board continued to
insist that it be done at that moment, and told her to open the cabinet. She
agreed that she was accountable to the Board but in good conscience could not
open the cabinet. At one point, Ms. Day told the Board that if they paid
severance, she would sue them for misappropriation because she believed they
would be using funds from O.W.L.’s “land and building” account which is a restricted
account containing funds from donors who made specific donations for that
purpose (O.W.L. had been looking to purchase land; the funds in the account
were also designated for the upkeep of bird cages). Ms. Day walked out of
the office where the meeting had taken place. It is possible that she uttered
the words, “you can fire me if you want to” when she refused to open the
cabinet. Ms. Wheatley admitted that after Ms. Day calmed down, she returned to
the meeting and she and the Board carried on with O.W.L.’s other business.

[
212
]

It was the only time in Ms. Day’s employment history with
O.W.L. that she ever refused to comply with a direction from the Board.

[
213
]

There was no need for the cheque to be signed at that moment since a
settlement with Mr. Hope had not yet been reached. No reasonable
explanation was provided by O.W.L. at trial for its insistence that the cheque
be issued at that moment or that Ms. Day be involved with it. If the Board
was adamant that a cheque be issued prior to concluding a settlement agreement,
then Board members could have easily had the cabinet opened the following day
by other persons with a key and obtained a cheque then (e.g., Ms. Hill). Or,
the Board could attend upon the bank directly and obtain a bank draft. The Board
minutes for the September 21 meeting reflect that two Board members would
attend at the bank on Monday to obtain a bank draft, which is what occurred the
following day.

[
214
]

During argument, Ms. Day’s counsel characterized the Board’s
approach to Ms. Day as provoking a confrontation with her, to force her to
do something they knew she was morally opposed to. It certainly appears that
way, particularly given the absence of any need, let alone urgency, for the
cheque to be signed at that moment. Mr. Hutchison’s evidence confirms that at
least he acted with that purpose. He confirmed in his evidence that he anticipated
that Ms. Day would refuse to provide a severance cheque to Mr. Hope.
It was readily apparent from his evidence that he expected Ms. Day would
react as she did to the Board’s direction. He also admitted that he assumed
that Irene Hill had keys to the cabinet, so that they did not need Ms. Day
to open it.

[
215
]

Mr. Hutchison testified that he was involved in the dismissal of Ms. Day
on the basis that she refused to follow a direct order of the Board to open the
filing cabinet. He also says he heard at a Board meeting that Ms. Day was
not paying her rent, which he saw as her taking O.W.L.’s money. He testified
that it factored into his determination that she should be dismissed,
commenting, “I didn’t trust her”. Yet, he was prepared to forgive the debt if
she resigned.

[
216
]

Mr. Hutchison’s animus to Ms. Day became so profound, that
he later called her, after other members of O.W.L. were petitioning for an
extraordinary general meeting of O.W.L.’s members to vote on whether the Board
should stay or resign, and told her that she was not allowed to come onto
O.W.L.’s premises and if she did, the police would be called and she would be
arrested. He made those comments, I find, without any reasonable basis to do
so, while she still resided on the property and was a member of O.W.L.

[
217
]

Insubordination includes a refusal to follow a direct instruction
from an employer. An employee’s wilful disobedience of a clear, reasonable, and
lawful order from an employer can provide a ground for summary dismissal:
Stein
v. British Columbia (Housing Management Commission)
, (1992),
1992 CanLII 4032 (BC CA)
, 65 B.C.L.R.
(2d) 181. To warrant dismissal for cause, the impugned conduct must constitute
a “complete disregard” of the “essential conditions of the contract of
service”:
Laws v. London Chronicle (Indicator Newspapers), Ltd.
,
[1959]
2 All E.R. 285 at 287 (C.A.)
, cited with approval in
Adams v. Fairmont
Hotels & Resorts Inc.
,
2009 BCSC 681
at paras.
277-278
. The
reasons for judgment in
Hayes v. First City Trust Co.
,
[1981] B.C.J. No.
1529 (S.C.)
refine the nature of insubordination required to justify summary
dismissal as a refusal to “carry out a policy or procedure well known by the
employee to be central to the fulfillment of the employer’s objectives.”
Hayes

was cited with approval by the Court of Appeal in
Panton
at para.

33
.

[
218
]

O.W.L. does not rely on insubordination on its own to provide a
basis to terminate Ms. Day’s employment for cause. Instead, it argued that
it was the cumulative effect of her refusal to follow the Board’s direction
concerning the chequebook and her non-payment of rent that led to the Board’s
determination that it could not trust her.

[
219
]

I have already determined that the rent issue does not afford O.W.L.
a ground for dismissal. Its defence concerning insubordination also fails. In
terms of insubordination, I have found that the Board could have readily
attended to the severance payment to Mr. Hope without involving
Ms. Day any further. I am satisfied that in issuing the order to Ms. Day,
which it knew she would object to, the Board sought to exert its authority over
Ms. Day in a wholly unnecessary manner guaranteed to generate conflict. Ms. Day
did not refuse to carry out a policy or procedure well known to Ms. Day or
O.W.L. or central to the fulfilment of its objectives.

[
220
]

Ms. Day had the authority to hire and fire employees. Having
issued numerous warnings to Mr. Hope, and dismissed him for engaging in
highly inappropriate conduct in front of staff and volunteers, the Board’s
order to Ms. Day to directly participate in the severance payment called
into question her authority and ongoing role as executive director that would
likely become known to staff and volunteers once the cheque was delivered to Mr. Hope.
I am satisfied that its decision to dismiss Ms. Day was grounded in the
Board’s dislike of Ms. Day’s continued objections to its decision to pay
severance to Mr. Hope.

[
221
]

Absent exceptional circumstances, which were not present in this
case, an isolated act of insubordination or insolence, particularly where the
employer provokes an avoidable confrontation, is not a basis for dismissal. The
impugned conduct must be examined in context and whether it is reconcilable
with sustaining the employment relationship:
Henry v. Foxco Ltd. (c.o.b. Fox
Ford)
,
2004 NBCA 22
at paras.
48-53
;
Thompson v. Lex Tec Inc.

(2001),
1490 A.C. 106 (C.A.)
.

[
222
]

The Board created an untenable situation for Ms. Day that did
not engage its right to dismiss her for insubordination. Her refusal to open
the cabinet and her threat to sue were singular isolated acts, out of keeping
with her exemplary performance to that date, based on her authority to fire and
her concern that O.W.L.’s funds in a segregated account would be improperly
used. Her conduct did not provide grounds for dismissal. It did not go to the
root of her employment contract with O.W.L. or fracture the employment
relationship. Once she calmed down, she carried on at the Board meeting to
attend to O.W.L.’s business. The Board’s decision to terminate Ms. Day was
not proportional to her response. A warning should have been given to Ms. Day.
Admissions during O.W.L.’s case made it clear that there was no prior history
of problems or concerns regarding Ms. Day’s management of O.W.L. or her
integrity, honesty, and treatment, supervision, and communications with
employees and volunteers other than alleged comments concerning Ms. Versteed
(which I discuss in a subsequent section). She was, by all accounts, a highly
regarded and revered founder of O.W.L., who was selflessly devoted to the
society and always acted with its best interests (as well as its staff and
volunteers) in mind. What I have gleaned from several comments made by Mr. Hutchison
and Ms. Wheatley in their evidence is that they were unhappy in their
belief that Ms. Day ran O.W.L. and treated the Board as essentially
superfluous. I took from their evidence that they wanted the Board to be the
primary decision-maker for O.W.L.

Summary

[
223
]

In summary, O.W.L. has failed to prove its grounds for dismissal concerning
Mr. Hope. Ms. Day did not make the accusations to Mr. Hope as he
alleged to the Board. She carried out a sufficient investigation before
dismissing Mr. Hope. She did not publish defamatory statements about Mr. Hope.
Her remarks concerning the basis of his dismissal were effectively limited to her
one-on-one meeting with Mr. Hope and to members of the Board (which were
protected by qualified privilege as there was no malice). It was Mr. Hope
who chose to publish an (inaccurate) account of Ms. Day’s comments to him
in his letter to the Board. Ms. Day did not prevent O.W.L. from issuing a
cheque to Mr. Hope. The Board had other means to access to the cabinet and
chequebook, and in any event, had separate access to O.W.L.’s bank accounts at
its financial institution.

[
224
]

I am also satisfied that Ms. Day did not intend to undermine
the relationship between the Board, O.W.L., and its employees. Her comment that
she would sue the Board for misappropriation, while not helpful in the
circumstances, was made in the heat of the moment out of her sincere belief
that the Board would be using money from a segregated account and that it was
acting illogically, exposing O.W.L. to criticism by the public and donors for
condoning a highly inappropriate incident, all to O.W.L.’s reputational and
financial detriment. Once she calmed down, Ms. Day returned to the Board
meeting and carried on attending to O.W.L.’s business. Her conduct did not
fracture the employment relationship. To dismiss Ms. Day based on her
decision not to open the filing cabinet is also not proportional in the
circumstances.

Neglecting Her Job Duties

[
225
]

There is no merit to O.W.L.’s claim that Ms. Day was
appropriately dismissed for neglecting her job duties “for several years prior
to her termination.”

[
226
]

O.W.L.’s own evidence, which I do not accept, suggests the issue
extends only as far back as spring 2014. There is no evidence to support O.W.L.’s
claim that Ms. Day’s work performance issues pre-date that time.

[
227
]

According to Ms. Wheatley, in the spring of 2014, she
challenged Ms. Day’s performance at work, after she received “complaints”
from staff that it was proving difficult to “move forward on some issues
because she wasn’t there.” No specifics were provided in Ms. Wheatley’s
testimony and no one other than Ms. Wheatley testified about this issue.
There is no reference in any of the Board minutes about Ms. Day neglecting
her job duties.

[
228
]

On Ms. Wheatley’s own evidence, she knew that Ms. Day’s
husband, Ralph Smith, who was on the Board at the time, was suffering from recently
diagnosed dementia and that Ms. Day was struggling to cope with his
illness.

[
229
]

To add to her plight, Ms. Day suffered from back pain that earlier
in 2014 had reduced her to using a walker at times. Nevertheless, Ms. Day
continued to work through her pain and attend to her duties at O.W.L.,
including her on call after hours work providing emergency treatment at her
on-site residence for injured birds.

[
230
]

To make matters worse, the day before Mr. Smith was due to be
discharged from the hospital, Ms. Day suffered a personal tragedy when her
daughter, who was a recovering addict, passed away on June 1, 2014. Her death
was “out of the blue”, Ms. Day said, since her daughter had been clean for
five years. According to Ms. Day, whose evidence I accept, when Mr. Smith
was being taken to the hospital, Ms. Wheatley told her that she should
“take as much time” off of work “that she needs”. Thus, for most of June 2014, Ms. Day
was occupied taking Mr. Smith to the hospital and medical appointments and
attending to her daughter’s funeral arrangements. In spite of this, Ms. Day
went to O.W.L.’s office to check on its operations and pay expenses, was always
available by telephone, and remained on call during the evenings.

[
231
]

Ms. Wheatley denied telling Ms. Day to take time away from
work. She testified that she knew Ms. Day was “going through a bit here with
Ralph,” yet told Ms. Day, “you know, O.W.L. needs you -- O.W.L. needs you here,
you know, to be able to function.” According to Ms. Wheatley, Ms. Day
should continue to work because as Ms. Wheatley put it, Ms. Day
“basically only lived 500 feet away from the office.” According to
Ms. Wheatley, she told Ms. Day that she should put Mr. Smith in a
care facility if he could not be left alone, “because you need to come to
work”.

[
232
]

O.W.L. did not have a short or long term disability policy for
employees at that time.

[
233
]

Even if I accepted Ms. Wheatley’s evidence on this issue, it
would not afford a basis for cause. Ms. Day was never warned that her
employment was in issue for taking personal time and spending less time
attending to work. Nor was Ms. Day warned that the two-week holiday she
took in August 2014, following the aftermath of events concerning
Mr. Smith and her daughter, would jeopardize her employment or that her
tenure as O.W.L.’s executive director was at stake.

[
234
]

To say that Ms. Day should be dismissed for cause in the
personal circumstances she found herself in at that time, in the absence of any
warning or less proportionate approach, and as she continued to attend to her
job duties as best as she could, is wholly without merit.

[
235
]

But as I said, I accept the evidence of Ms. Day and find that
her decreased hours from her work duties in the summer of 2014 was encouraged
and condoned by O.W.L., and there is no basis for termination:
Hennessy

at paras.
12-13
;
Nicholls v. Columbia Taping Tools Ltd.
,
2013 BCSC
2201
;
Poirer v. Wal-Mart Canada Corp.
,
2006 BCSC 1138
at para.
48
.

[
236
]

Ms. Wheatley continued to take a dim view of Ms. Day’s
work performance. Following Ms. Day’s protests over the Board’s decision
to pay severance to Mr. Hope. In August 2014, Ms. Wheatley instructed
a junior office clerk to keep a record of Ms. Day’s attendances at
O.W.L.’s office. Ms. Day was unaware that her appearances in the office were
being recorded. The clerk was asked to make detailed notes of the time of Ms. Day’s
arrivals and departures, including any time Ms. Day went outside to have a
cigarette break. Ms. Wheatley’s reliance on these notes ignores Ms. Day’s
personal circumstances and fails to recognize that the clerk’s notes did not
track the times that Ms. Day was out of the office but working elsewhere
on the property or off site dealing with O.W.L.’s business or her hours spent
on call attending to bird rescues. In addition, the employee who kept the notes
testified that she did not fully understand Ms. Day’s role at O.W.L. She
also admitted that her notes may not be complete for every single day or hour.

[
237
]

Mr. Myran, who opened the premises in the morning and worked
throughout the facility, confirmed seeing Ms. Day on site throughout the
property during her employment in 2014. I accept his testimony that even when Ms. Day
was dealing with the aftermath of her daughter’s death and her husband’s
dementia (which was diagnosed in June 2014), he continued to receive
instructions from her on a regular basis and met with her to review work
required for O.W.L. and the type of building materials that should be bought.

[
238
]

I reject O.W.L.’s submission that its resort to tracking Ms. Day’s
attendance was not connected to her termination of Mr. Hope’s employment.
The clerk who was asked to keep the notes testified that “shortly around the
time that” Mr. Hope was dismissed, she was approached by a Board member to
record “Ms. Day’s comings and goings”. I took it from the clerk’s
testimony that she saw the direction as something she had to follow as an
employee of O.W.L. but was nevertheless a matter of politics at O.W.L. that she
did not like to get involved with.

[
239
]

I also have considerable concerns about the credibility and
reliability of Ms. Wheatley’s testimony in respect of this issue. It was
not based on any first hand or personal knowledge of Ms. Day’s performance
of her duties, but seemingly only on what she heard from other unidentified
persons. None of Ms. Wheatley’s concerns are recorded in Board minutes or
in any written document. The nature and tone of her testimony vacillated between,
on the one hand, sympathy and on the other, indifference to Ms. Day’s
personal circumstances.

[
240
]

O.W.L. did not lead any other evidence to establish that
Ms. Day was not fulfilling her job duties for O.W.L.

[
241
]

Even if I had accepted Ms. Wheatley’s testimony, it would not
support a basis for dismissal with cause. If Ms. Day had been neglecting
her job duties, it was only for a brief period of approximately two to three
months, and not for several years as pleaded. Also, there was no warning given
to Ms. Day that she may be subject to discipline or that her job may be in
jeopardy. Further, a warning of that nature would be highly inappropriate in
the particular personal circumstances Ms. Day found herself in, especially
given her longstanding history of exemplary service with O.W.L.

[
242
]

I also found Ms. Wheatley’s covert measure to track Ms. Day’s
attendance to be inexplicable in these circumstances, particularly after her
daughter’s death and Mr. Smith’s recent diagnosis of dementia. I agree with Ms.
Day’s submission that I can infer from this conduct a motive to find evidence
harmful to Ms. Day in light of her objection to the Board’s decision to
pay severance to Mr. Hope. One of Ms. Day’s submissions was that Ms. Wheatley
appeared to be trying to build a case against her when she instructed a junior
clerk to track her attendance at O.W.L.’s office. From my observations of Ms. Wheatley
while testifying, the manner and tone of her testimony, and after having
considered the totality of the circumstances, I have reached the same factual
conclusion.

Martina Versteed

[
243
]

The impugned incident occurred in 2013 when Ms. Day, Ms. Versteed,
and Rob Hope were standing outside in the smoking area. Rob and Ms. Versteed
told Ms. Day of her pregnancy, and that it occurred because they had “gone
out partying”, “got high”, and forgot to use protection. Ms. Day was
surprised because she was not aware that the two of them were living together.
In light of Ms. Versteed’s apparent chagrin, Ms. Day recited, in a
sing-song voice, what she described as a “ditty” she heard from her mother:

My momma done
told me that if I was going out to get drunk or drink to make sure I always
kept my legs crossed.

[
244
]

I accept Ms. Day’s evidence that she meant no offence by her
remarks and was simply trying to lighten the mood. At the same time, they were
inappropriate in the context of an employer-employee relationship, especially
where Ms. Day had issued a formal written warning to Ms. Versteed in
October 2012 for failing to treat “some co-workers or volunteers with the
respect they deserve.”

[
245
]

Mr. Myran walked in at the end of their conversation and heard Ms. Versteed,
Mr. Hope, and Ms. Day all laughing. The only part of the conversation
he heard was a comment about legs being crossed. Mr. Myran also confirmed
that no one else was present. He was not certain if Ms. Versteed was
pregnant at the time or had given birth to her child, but confirmed that she
did not have a child with her. He also said that Ms. Day did not tell Ms. Versteed
that she could not return to work.

[
246
]

I reject Ms. Wheatley’s account of the incident, where she
described Ms. Day as having told Ms. Versteed, in response to the
latter’s request to return to her pre-maternity hours, that she “should have
thought about that before you spread your legs”. Ms. Wheatley’s evidence
that Ms. Versteed had her child on her lap at the time was refuted by the
evidence of Ms. Day and Mr. Myran. Ms. Wheatley’s evidence,
including her evidence describing it “as the most outrageous thing I’ve ever
actually heard come out of somebody’s mouth in a work environment,” smacked of
emotive hyperbole, particularly in circumstances where Ms. Wheatley did
not seem troubled by Mr. Hope’s involvement in the incident with Mr. Myran
with minors and other staff in the room. If Ms. Wheatley was as offended
as she claimed (and she did not testify as to any response made by Ms. Versteed),
it would be expected, in her role on the Board, that she would take up the
issue with the Board or issue a formal reprimand to Ms. Day, or both. She
did neither.

[
247
]

Ms. Day heard nothing about the incident until it was raised as
a ground for her dismissal over one year later. Nor was Ms. Day ever
provided with a warning about that incident or any other inappropriate
communications with staff or Board members. The ground asserted by O.W.L.
appears to have been raised as an after-thought, and conflated with a separate
incident where Ms. Day and Ms. Versteed discussed returning to work
from maternity leave, in order to buttress the case for dismissal.

[
248
]

Like the incident involving Mr. Hope, there was no credible
evidence tendered on behalf of O.W.L. to challenge Ms. Day’s account of
events. According to Ms. Wheatley, two other employees were in the room at
the time, Mr. Hope and Mindy Dyck. O.W.L. did not call them to testify,
nor did it call Ms. Versteed.

[
249
]

While I find Ms. Day’s comments to Ms. Versteed as she
explained them in her evidence to have been highly inappropriate, in the
absence of any warning or evidence establishing a pattern of similar
inappropriate conduct, they do not afford a ground for dismissal with cause.

Dismissal

[
250
]

The termination letter was handed to Ms. Day by Ms. Wheatley
and Mr. Hutchison on October 23, 2014, which according to O.W.L.’s notice of
civil claim (at para. 17), was approximately four days after it discovered
the rent issue. Ms. Day was given the termination letter at O.W.L.’s office,
where staff were present elsewhere in the office. Ms. Day’s response was
that they could not “fire me” since she believed that the Board was required to
take the matter before a committee of her peers and then to the members at an
annual general meeting. She was given two months’ notice to vacate her home and
leave the premises. She left the meeting.

[
251
]

After Ms. Day was dismissed, she reimbursed O.W.L. for the rent
of her accommodation in the amount of $750 per month (the $100 per month
increase followed upon Ms. Wheatley’s negotiations with the landlord when
the lease was renewed in late September 2014). O.W.L. invoiced Ms. Day
each month on the basis that it was facilitating payment of Ms. Day’s rent to
the landlord on her behalf.

[
252
]

When the Board terminated Ms. Day’s employment, Ms. Wheatley
immediately contacted the landlord to advise that O.W.L. did not require Ms.
Day’s residence any further.

Summary

[
253
]

None of the grounds advanced by O.W.L. constitute just cause for the
dismissal of Ms. Day.

Damages

Notice Period

[
254
]

Ms. Day seeks an award of 30 months’ severance on the basis
that her circumstances fall within the category of “exceptional” cases that
exceed the general “rough upper limit” of 24 months:
Webster v. British Columbia
Hydro and Power Authority
(1990),
1992 CanLII 1087 (BC CA)
, 91 D.L.R. (4th) 272 at 276-77 (B.C.C.A),
aff’d
1994 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 549, citing
Ansari v. British Columbia Hydro and Power
Authority
(1986),
1986 CanLII 1023 (BC SC)
, 2 B.C.L.R. (2d) 33 (S.C.), aff’d 55 B.C.L.R. (2d) xxxiii
(C.A.)
Sorel v. Tomlinson Saunders Whitehead Ltd
(1997),
1987 CanLII 154 (BC CA)
, 15 B.C.L.R. (2d)
38 at 42 (C.A.) and
Suttie v. Metro Transit Operating Co.
(1986),
1985 CanLII 525 (BC CA)
, 2
B.C.L.R. (2d) 145 (C.A.)
.
In her submission, the upper limit should be
increased in light of the length she held her senior position as executive
director of O.W.L. (both as a salaried employee and paid by stipend), her
highly specialized field, and her age. O.W.L.’s position is that an appropriate
range for the notice period is between 12 to 15 months.

[
255
]

The applicable principles in determining an
appropriate award for damages in a wrongful dismissal case are described in
many cases, including the Supreme Court of Canada in its decision in
Keays
v. Honda Canada Inc.
,
2008 SCC 39
, where it re-affirmed the four factors
set out in
Bardal v. The Globe & Mail Ltd.
(1960),
1960 CanLII 294 (ON HCJ)
, 24 D.L.R. (2d)
140 (Ont. H.C.) at paras.
28-29
:

[28]      In determining what constitutes
reasonable notice of termination, the courts have generally applied the
principles articulated by McRuer C.J.H.C. in
Bardal
, at p. 145:

There can be no
catalogue laid down as to what is reasonable notice in particular classes of
cases. The reasonableness of the notice must be decided with reference to each
particular case, having regard to the character of the employment, the length
of service of the servant, the age of the servant and the availability of
similar employment, having regard to the experience, training and
qualifications of the servant.

[29]      These four factors
were adopted by this Court in
Machtinger v. HOJ Industries Ltd.
,
1992 CanLII 102 (SCC)
, [1992]
1 S.C.R. 986. They can only be determined on a case by case basis.

[
256
]

The individual circumstances of the employee, including the nature
and duties of their job, are at the forefront of the court’s analysis. No one factor
is to be given disproportionate weight:
Honda
at paras. 31-32. A
dismissed employee facing a known limited employment market will generally be
entitled to a longer notice period:
Schamborzki v. North Shore Health Region
,

2000 BCSC 1573
at para.
30
.

[
257
]

I agree with O.W.L.’s submission that it is the
character of the employment of the individual that is relevant, not the title
associated with that position. It is incorrect to say, as O.W.L. does however,
that Ms. Day “spent her time primarily in overseeing staff” of six paid
staff and “many volunteers”. The submission overlooks her responsibility to
manage the overall operations of O.W.L. as well as her ongoing and substantive fundraising
and public relations activities (both on and off site) and bird rescue
activities which mainly occurred after hours at night. I agree with
Ms. Day that given the length and nature of her position with O.W.L. as
its founder and head of its operations for approximately 30 years (including her
18-year tenure as its paid executive director in charge of all of its
operations) and her narrow field of expertise, her circumstances fall within
the category of exceptional cases justifying an award beyond two years.

[
258
]

For those reasons as well as her age at the time
of dismissal (63), I would award 26 months having regard to case authorities
cited on behalf of Ms. Day in closing argument (i.e.,
Lowndes v. Summit
Ford Sales Ltd.
(2006),
2006 CanLII 14 (ON CA)
, 206 O.A.C. 55 (C.A.);
Keenan v. Canac Kitchens
Ltd.
,
2016 ONCA 79
;
Cardenas v. Canac Kitchens
,
[2009] O.J. No. 1570
(S.C.J.)
). The cases cited by O.W.L. in respect of the notice period do not, in
my respectful opinion, align with Ms. Day’s circumstances in this case.

[
259
]

Ms. Day has also lost vacation pay at 6% of her annual salary.
She is also entitled to that amount.

[
260
]

However, the length of the notice period is affected by
Ms. Day’s evidence that she had hoped to reduce her hours over time given
her husband’s medical condition. To allow for her admitted intention to reduce
her hours at some point in time if possible (and its corresponding affect on
her salary), it is appropriate in my opinion to deduct two months from the
notice period to account for that likely contingency. It is also appropriate to
apply it to her entitlement to vacation pay to account for its corresponding
reduction to a reduced salary. Since Ms. Day would still be entitled to
employer paid medical and dental benefits as an employee even with reduced
hours, I would not apply the contingency to those and certain other lost
benefits.

[
261
]

Ms. Day testified that her termination almost caused a breakdown
in her marriage and increased stress and anxiety, with consequential insomnia
and weight loss. She suffered social isolation in light of the misappropriation
allegations and from being prohibited entry to O.W.L. To Ms. Day, O.W.L.
and its staff and volunteers were her family. Saving injured raptors was her
life’s work. Ms. Day continues to be contacted by police and firefighters
and others after she was terminated, and she directs them to O.W.L. She directs
those and all other enquiries to O.W.L. and has changed her answering machine
at home, advising people to contact O.W.L. directly. She is upset that she is
not allowed by O.W.L. to be involved in bird rescues. She is also upset that as
a member of O.W.L. she has been told that she cannot attend its premises. Her
loss in these respects has caused her to suffer additional stress requiring
additional medication.

[
262
]

She suffered further distress when she had no income coming in until
she was eligible for government assistance when she turned 65. She used her
savings to pay for medical bills, prescriptions, and legal fees, and sold her
vehicle. She now lives off her government pension.

[
263
]

While I accept Ms. Day’s evidence in those respects, her health
issues, and likewise, her ongoing distress and wounded feelings suffered as a
consequence of being dismissed are not part of the calculation of the
appropriate notice period:
Honda
at paras. 56-57, 59. Those factors
may, however, be considered in determining her claim for aggravated damages.
Otherwise, damages are confined to the loss suffered as a result of the
employer’s failure to provide proper notice:
Honda
at para. 50,
citing
Addis v. Gramophone Co.
,
[1909] A.C. 488 (H.L.)
.

Failure to Mitigate

[
264
]

O.W.L.’s position is that Ms. Day failed to mitigate her loss. The
onus, which is a heavy one, is on O.W.L. to prove what Ms. Day might
reasonably have earned following her dismissal:
Evans v. Teamsters Local Union
No. 31
,
2008 SCC 20
at paras.
30
, 97-100, 106, 113-115, 137;
Red
Deer College v. Michaels
,
1975 CanLII 15 (SCC)
, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 324 at 331-332, 346-347;
Szczypiorkowski
v. Coast Capital Savings Credit Union
,
2011 BCSC 1376
at para.
90
. The
employee’s obligation to mitigate is assessed in context and is measured on the
standard of reasonableness:
Forshaw v. Aluminex Extrusions Ltd.
(1989),

1989 CanLII 234 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 140 (C.A.);
Gryba v. Moneta Porcupine Mines Ltd.
(2000),

2000 CanLII 16997 (ON CA)
, 5 C.C.E.L. (3d) 43 at paras.
56-57
(Ont. C.A.), leave to appeal to SCC refused,
[2001] S.C.C.A. No. 92. The duty to act reasonably does not require the
dismissed employee to accept lower paying or markedly inferior or menial work:
Forshaw

at 6-7;
Sunderarajah v. Metro Toronto Condominium Corp. No. 748

(2005),
2005 CanLII 5358 (ON SC)
, 46 C.C.E.L. (3d) 309 (Ont. S.C.J.), leave to appeal to the C.A. refused,

[2005] O.J. No. 2509
. Moreover, an employee need not embark upon a job
search immediately following dismissal. Some “recovery time” to deal with the
impact of dismissal is appropriate; each case must be assessed on its
particular facts, including the dismissed employee’s physical and mental
condition:
Systad v. Ray-Mont Logistics Canada Inc.
,
2011 BCSC 1202
at para.
31
;

Robinson v. Team Cooperheat-MQS Canada Inc.
,
2008 ABQB 409
at paras.
120-121
.

[
265
]

I disagree with O.W.L.’s submission that it has established
availability of similar employment for Ms. Day. It has adduced any evidence of
available employment or labour market opportunities. The only evidence came
from Ms. Day and it concerned possible employment with other
rehabilitation facilities that cared for different types of animals for which
Ms. Day lacked expertise, appropriate experience, or training.

[
266
]

Thus, the evidence O.W.L. relies upon comes from Ms. Day who
testified that she received several enquiries after her dismissal from other
animal welfare societies, expressing an interest in having her join them. No
evidence was adduced to establish the particulars, including the nature of any
potential employment or salary. O.W.L. did not explore particulars in
cross-examination. Ms. Day’s evidence that the type of work was something where
she had no experience or expertise was unchallenged. Otherwise, the matter was
left as vague. From the evidence, I have concluded that those approaches involved
expressions of interest and a couple of tentative invitations of a vague nature
which were not equivalent to the type of employment she had with O.W.L.

[
267
]

O.W.L. has not established from Ms. Day that she rejected job offers
of suitable employment. The most it has established is from Ms. Day’s own voluntary
and candid admission (which typified the nature of her testimony) that she has
not looked for work since she was dismissed. According to Ms. Day, she needed
time to recover from surgery (which took place in early 2015) and from the
angst of her dismissal. She was also caught up in dealing with the unfounded
misappropriation related allegations and believed this case would be over
quickly.

[
268
]

In
Systad
, Mr. Justice Burnyeat held at para. 32 that the
combination of the employee’s initial period of shock from dismissal and his
subsequent knee surgery coupled with the need for possible future medical
interventions resulted in the employer’s failure to establish a failure to
mitigate defence.

[
269
]

Similar circumstances concerning an employee’s inadequate efforts to
look for work arose in
Coyes v. Ocelot Industries Ltd.
(1984),
1984 CanLII 1191 (AB QB)
, 56 A.R.
241 (Q.B.). In that case, the court held that the employer failed to meet its
onus to establish a failure to mitigate defence on the evidence in spite of the
employee’s deficient efforts. A dismissed employee’s lack of effort to look for
employment was also established in
Robinson
, but in that case, the
employer met its onus by adducing evidence “demonstrating a vibrant labour
market”: para. 123.

[
270
]

There is no doubt that apart from the issues she faces with
Mr. Smith, Ms. Day is currently able to work. She admitted that her
back issues have improved considerably following her recovery from spinal
fusion surgery. The difficulty she faces at the present time is with her age
(now 68), her limited area of expertise, and the amount of time she spends
caring for Mr. Smith. Ms. Day is currently unable to leave Mr. Smith
unattended. He now requires full-time attention to avoid mishaps (for example,
he gets lost easily and has left gas burners turned on the stove when left on
his own). These current issues involving Mr. Smith fall outside the notice
period and do not bear on the failure to mitigate defence.

[
271
]

I have not been taken to any cases where an employer established a
failure to mitigate defence solely on the basis of the dismissed employee’s
admission that he or she did not look for work following their dismissal.

[
272
]

While I would not wish my decision to in any way be seen to
encourage dismissed employees not to look for work, I am left with no other conclusion
than O.W.L. has failed to prove a failure to mitigate defence.

[
273
]

Accordingly, Ms. Day shall have judgment for 24 months of
annual salary of $41,424.00 plus vacation pay at 6% for that period.

at

18-20
, 37;

at 44;

[

]
