Aggravated and Punitive Damages

[
284
]

Ms. Day claims for damages beyond her actual losses, arising
from what she alleges was O.W.L.’s breach of its obligation to act in good
faith and fair dealing, both in respect of her dismissal and its post-dismissal
conduct. She seeks aggravated and punitive damages. Aggravated damages are
distinct from punitive damages. The former is intended to compensate the
victim. Punitive damages, on the other hand, are not meant to be compensatory
but instead are awarded to punish the wrongdoer.

Aggravated Damages

[
285
]

In wrongful dismissal cases, damages for hurt feelings or emotional
distress arising from the loss of the job are not normally recoverable. Employers
are expected to act in good faith in the course of the dismissal. Aggravated
damages are awarded for mental distress suffered by the dismissed employee in
exceptional circumstances where the nature of the employer’s conduct, either in
the manner of the dismissal or subsequent to it, has been unfair, untruthful,
misleading, unduly insensitive (such as persisting in wrongful allegations of
dishonest conduct), misrepresenting the reasons for the termination, or firing
an employee who is on disability leave, or is otherwise in bad faith, has
caused additional harm to the dismissed employee. An actionable wrong
independent of the dismissal is not a necessary pre-condition to the award. An
award of aggravated damages is intended to be compensatory. It is for a fixed
amount as opposed to an extension of the notice period:
Honda
at paras. 53-60;

Doyle v. Zochem Inc.
,
2017 ONCA 130
at para.
12
. Aggravated damages
are not subject to deduction for an employee’s failure to mitigate:
Evans

at
para.
32
.

[
286
]

Employer conduct during termination as well as after have been
considered by courts in determining whether to award aggravated damages so long
as the conduct is relevant to the dismissal:
Coppola v. Capital Pontiac
Buick Cadillac GMC Ltd.
,
2011 SKQB 318
at para.
58
, aff’d
2013 SKCA 80
;

Gismondi v. Toronto (City)
(2003),
2003 CanLII 52143 (ON CA)
, 64 O.R. (3d) 688 at paras.
23
, 27-32 (C.A.);

Silvester v. Lloyds’ Register North America Inc.
,
2003 NSSC 84
at paras.

51
, 53-54, appeal allowed in part
2004 NSCA 17
at paras.
23-28
;
Marshall v.
Watson Wyatt & Co. (c.o.b. Watson Wyatt Worldwide)
(
2002),
2002 CanLII 13354 (ON CA)
, 57 O.R. (3d)
813 at paras.
40-41
;
Pate Estate v. Galway-Cavendish (Township)
,
2013
ONCA 669
;
Doyle
at para.
13
;
Karmel v. Calgary Jewish Academy
,

2015 ABQB 731
at paras.
91-99
.
Doyle
and
Karmel
were decided
after
Honda
and support Ms. Day’s submission that
Honda
does
not exclude post-termination conduct as a basis for an award.

[
287
]

In
Bailey

v. Service Corporation
International (Canada) ULC
,
2018 BCSC 235
at para.
205
, Griffin J., as
she then was, described the applicable principles for an award of aggravated
damages:

The Court of Appeal recently discussed
aggravated damages in the context of an employment case in
Lau v. Royal
Bank of Canada
,
2017 BCCA 253
[
Lau
]. From
Lau
and the
authorities it cites including the leading Supreme Court of Canada cases of
Wallace
v. United Grain Growers Limited
,
1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 701, 152 D.L.R. (4th) 1 [
Wallace
],
and
Honda Canada Inc. v. Keays
,
2008 SCC 39
[
Honda
], a number of
principles emerge:

1.

A
person’s work is a significant aspect of a person’s life, key to self-worth.

2.

Employers
have an obligation of good faith and fair dealing in the manner of dismissal of
an employee. This includes refraining from conduct that is untruthful,
misleading or unduly insensitive (
Wallace
at paras.
95 and 98
).

3.

When the
employment relationship ends, the employee is vulnerable and some upset can be
expected. Normal upset that can be expected is not compensable. However,
aggravated damages resulting from the manner of dismissal are available if they
result from conduct that is unfair or in bad faith (
Honda
at paras. 56,
57).

4.

Examples
of facts which can give rise to aggravated damages include but are not
limited to conduct that is untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive. Other
conduct in which aggravated damages may be awarded include maintaining wrongful
allegations of dishonest conduct; misrepresenting the reason for the
termination; and firing an employee who is on disability leave (
Lau
at para.
31
).

5.

Aggravated
damages are compensatory based on foreseeable injury for breach of the duty of
good faith and fairness. Because of this there must be some evidence that the
manner of dismissal (as opposed to the mere fact of dismissal) is the cause of
damaging effects on the dismissed employee, whether mental distress or
intangible effects such as damage to reputation (
Lau
at paras.
54,
59-60, 62
).

6.

Medical evidence is not necessary to award aggravated damages based
on mental distress caused by the manner of dismissal but there must be some
evidence that transcends ordinary upset or distress (
Lau
at para.
49
).
This can include evidence from the employee or from family members or friends.

[
288
]

Ms. Day advanced numerous grounds of misconduct on O.W.L.’s
part to support her claim for an award of aggravated damages. The list of
grounds on which I have determined an award of aggravated damages should be
made in this case includes those advanced on behalf of Ms. Day that I
found compelling, as follows (and not in any particular order):

(a)       without conducting an adequate investigation accusing Ms. Day,
both in the termination letter and the pleadings filed in this action (and available
to the public) of dishonest conduct when claiming that she misappropriated
O.W.L.’s funds;

(b)       pursuing the misappropriation claim through to the close
of evidence at trial without conducting an adequate investigation and in the
face of its own documents;

(c)        doggedly persisting in a “continuum of conduct” to
castigate Ms. Day through to the conclusion of trial, including labelling
her conduct in respect of the unjust enrichment claim as “purposeful” “financial
mismanagement” even though it abandoned the misappropriation claim;

(d)       laying unfounded allegations of poor performance, neglect
of her job duties, and intentional misconduct that were made public and that
cast a shadow on Ms. Day’s character and reputation;

(e)       persisting in its allegations that Ms. Day failed in
her duty to investigate before terminating Mr. Hope’s employment and
misappropriating funds and neglected her job duties, in a thoughtless [and to
that I would add, reckless] manner;

(f)         advancing
allegations in its filed trial brief, which is also a public document, with the
following allegations, without any basis to do so:

a.         the
defendant [Ms. Day] in her role as executive director treated the
Society’s [O.W.L.’s] money as her own;

b.         she
used her unfettered discretion to pay her personal rent without authorization,
vacation pay and salary increases;

c.         these
actions were purposefully hid from the Board or presented to the Board with
information that prevented them from being able to identify these actions on
her part;

d.         the defendant
used her position as Executive Director to further her own personal agenda.

(g)       callous and insensitive treatment (such as threatening to
have her arrested if she attended at the premises and terminating her
employment at a time she was suffering personal hardship without conducting an
adequate investigation);

(h)        encouraging Ms. Day to take time off of work and
then using her purported absences as a ground for dismissal;

(i)         unnecessarily directing her to participate in the
payment of severance to Mr. Hope when it knew that she would object and
then using it as a ground for dismissal;

(j)         instructing a junior clerk to keep track of Ms. Day’s
attendance at the office without instructing the clerk to keep the matter
confidential, while knowing that Ms. Day’s duties for O.W.L. took her
outside the office building to elsewhere (on O.W.L.’s property and off the
property) during regular business hours and knowing that she was on call
through the evenings and nights for bird rescues, and then using the clerk’s record,
which by the clerk’s own admission did not portray an accurate account, to inaccurately
portray Ms. Day as neglecting her duties; and

(k)        requiring Ms. Day to move out of her home on two
months’ notice at a time when she was suffering grief and hardship due to the
death of her daughter and her husband’s ill health.

[
289
]

To those grounds, I would add Ms. Day’s role with O.W.L. was a
significant and consuming part of her life and sense of self-worth and her
vulnerability at the time of termination and thereafter as she was forced to
defend meritless claims concerning her honesty and character. It was more than
her 30-year vocation with O.W.L. Her life’s work and purpose were intimately
tied with O.W.L. She was more than the public face of O.W.L. For herself and to
the public, she was O.W.L.’s driving force. She has suffered emotional and
physical distress from the nature of the grounds O.W.L. advanced for her
dismissal along with O.W.L.’s dogged pursuit of its meritless claim for
unauthorized payments and defences to her wrongful dismissal claim.

[
290
]

I accept Ms. Day’s evidence that O.W.L.’s conduct has
significantly aggravated and substantially worsened the emotional and physical
distress that she suffered from her daughter’s death and continues to suffer
from her husband’s dementia. I accept Ms. Day’s evidence that her relationship
with her husband has also been adversely impacted at times as Ms. Day has
struggled to defend the case brought by O.W.L. and defend her character,
integrity, competence, and reputation. I am able to make these findings on the
evidence and in the absence of medical opinion evidence:
Bailey

at para.

205
(sub-para. 6).

[
291
]

In spite of my concern that Ms. Day was terminated in the office
where other employees were present, I agree with O.W.L. that there is no basis
to award damages in respect of the actual discussion at the termination meeting
itself. The meeting between Ms. Day and Ms. Wheatley and Mr. Hutchison
was uneventful and short. They handed her a termination letter and told her
that she was dismissed. Otherwise, I am satisfied that the other circumstances as
outlined above justify an award.

[
292
]

In terms of the quantum of the award, counsel for Ms. Day cited
a number of cases setting out a range between $50,000 and $200,000, including
Downham
v. Lennox (County)
(2005),
2005 CanLII 45197 (ON SC)
, 56 C.C.E.L. (3d) 112 (Ont. S.C.J.);
Doyle
;
and
Karmel
.

Those cases review other case authorities with both
lower and higher awards.

[
293
]

Each of those three cases involved employer misconduct involved
inadequate investigations and ongoing allegations of employee misconduct up to
trial that had no basis in fact that the employer should have known were
untrue. O.W.L.’s conduct was similar in nature. While O.W.L. can argue that it
relied on Ms. Day’s initial position in the case that her rent was
supposed to be deducted from her paycheques, by the time the prior Board
minutes were in hand, it should have been clear to O.W.L. that its unjust
enrichment claim concerning rent was wholly without merit and the amended
position taken by Ms. Day was correct. It chose instead to pursue a claim
of purposeful financial mismanagement, of varying dollar amounts, that was at
odds with its pleading, and it continued to do so as its own evidence was being
adduced in its case. O.W.L.’s conduct in that respect moved from indifferent to
reckless. The public nature of its efforts to obtain judgment and its defences
to the counterclaim all cast meritless doubt on Ms. Day’s integrity,
character, and ability to perform her job duties at O.W.L. and have significantly
compounded the distress suffered by Ms. Day that went beyond, as Griffin
J. said in
Bailey
at para.
205
(3), the upset typically expected.

[
294
]

Proof of the distress and the effect of O.W.L.’s dismissal and
post-dismissal conduct came from Ms. Day, all of which I found credible (she
was prevented from admitting into evidence a letter from her family doctor as a
result of O.W.L.’s objection based on lack of appropriate notice).

[
295
]

Without in any way intending to diminish the inappropriate nature of
O.W.L.’s conduct, I am of the opinion that Ms. Day’s pre-existing distress
caused by her personal circumstances unrelated to her dismissal must be taken
into account in assessing an appropriate award. In the circumstances, and in
the absence of any admissible medical opinion evidence, I have determined that
an appropriate award in this case is $30,000.

Punitive Damages

[
296
]

Three requirements must be met to obtain an award for punitive
damages in the context of a breach of contract:
Whiten v. Pilot Insurance
Co.
,
2002 SCC 18
at paras.
36
, 74, 78;
Boucher v. Wal-Mart Canada
Corp.
,
2014 ONCA 419
at paras.
79-80
.

[
297
]

The first requirement focuses on the employer’s conduct. Many case
authorities hold that the employer’s conduct must have been harsh, vindictive, reprehensible,
malicious, oppressive, or high-handed and constitute a marked departure from
ordinary standards of decent behaviour. However, more recently, in
Honda
,
which concerned a wrongful dismissal case, the Court appeared to limit the
categories of impugned conduct, stating that “punitive damages are restricted
to advertent wrongful acts that are so malicious and outrageous that they are
deserving of punishment on their own”: para. 62. The second requirement is
that the employer committed an “actionable wrong”, which does not require proof
of a separate tort but can include a breach of the employer’s contractual duty
to act in good faith:
Honda
at para. 62;
Boucher
at para.
81
;

Whiten

at paras.
78-82
. The third requirement is that an award must
be rationally required to punish the wrongdoer and must meet the objectives of
retribution, deterrence and denunciation:
Boucher
at para.
79
.

[
298
]

Ms. Day submits she has met those tests. Her claim for punitive
damages is premised on many of the same grounds advanced for aggravated
damages.

[
299
]

Ms. Day has not proven actual malice either in the grounds
advanced or in bringing the action. Nor do I think this is a case where, as Ms. Day’s
counsel urged me to find, that the requirements for malicious prosecution have
been made out.

[
300
]

Ms. Day has proven that some of O.W.L.’s conduct in relation to
the dismissal in terms of the grounds asserted at the time of dismissal and
thereafter, as well as O.W.L.’s conduct post-dismissal (but not the meeting
involving the dismissal itself) have been harsh and oppressive, and sometimes high-handed
and reprehensible. Reckless pursuit of meritless claims also constitutes a
marked departure from ordinary standards of decent behaviour. But those
matters, such as O.W.L.’s continued allegation of purposeful financial
mismanagement even after it abandoned the claim for misappropriation and heard
the evidence of O.W.L.’s former Board members and bookkeepers, are in my
opinion, more appropriately taken into account in this case in assessing
aggravated damages.

[
301
]

Honda
cautions that claims for punitive
damages should “receive the most careful consideration” and its discretion
should be “cautiously exercised”; double-compensation of “double-punishment”
must be avoided where aggravated damages have been awarded: paras. 60, 68.
I am also mindful of the Court’s statement in
Whiten
that punitive
damages are awarded “‘if, but only if”
all
other penalties have been
taken into account and found to be inadequate to accomplish the objectives of
retribution, deterrence, and denunciation”: para. 123 (emphasis in original).

[
302
]

I am cognizant that Ms. Day intends to seek special costs
arising for some of the same matters she claims supports an award of punitive
damages, i.e., O.W.L.’s abandonment of the misappropriation claim just before
argument began and for what she has described as reprehensible conduct during
the litigation, and am aware that punitive damages and special costs should not
be conflated:
Kelly v. Norsemont Mining Inc.
,
2013 BCSC 17
at para.
147
.
I am therefore reluctant to conclude that no other penalty is inadequate to
accomplish the objectives underlying punitive damages. Accordingly, I am of the
opinion that no award for punitive damages should be made.

Summary

[
303
]

O.W.L.’s claim against Ms. Day is dismissed.

304
]

lost annual salary of $41,424.00, plus lost

for 26 months);

(d)

lost employer-paid contribution to MSP premiums

305
]

[
306
]

Court Order
Interest Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 79, on her award of lost salary and

Interest Act
.

307
]
